entities.name: Khazret Sultan Mosque
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Khazret Sultan Mosque, inaugurated on July 6, 2012, in Astana, Kazakhstan, stands as the largest mosque in Central Asia, symbolizing a resurgence of Islamic heritage in a region historically influenced by various empires and religions. It was designed by the Turkish architect Zeynep Fadillioglu, who was chosen for her expertise in creating modern yet culturally resonant religious structures. The mosque can accommodate 10,000 worshippers and features a stunning 80-meter-high dome, making it a landmark not only in Kazakhstan but throughout Asia, reflecting the country’s aspiration to blend modernity with tradition.

The construction of the Khazret Sultan Mosque was part of a broader initiative to promote Islam's significance and cultural identity in Kazakhstan, especially following its independence from the Soviet Union in 1991. This monumental mosque serves not only as a house of worship but also as a center for cultural events, educational programs, and interfaith dialogues. Its design incorporates traditional Kazakh elements, such as intricate tile work and calligraphy, while utilizing contemporary architectural techniques, thus bridging past and present.

The legacy of the Khazret Sultan Mosque extends beyond its physical presence; it has invigorated the local Muslim community and played a critical role in the country's national identity. As Kazakhstan positions itself as a leader in promoting peace and dialogue among religions, the mosque has become a symbol of unity and cultural pride. Its establishment has also encouraged the construction of other religious and cultural institutions, fostering a renaissance of Islamic architecture in the region.
